Jupiter.lead: The largest planet, about 143,000 kilometers across at the equator.
Jupiter.story: Its Great Red Spot is a storm bigger than Earth, and a whole day there passes in under ten hours.

claims.text: about 143,000 kilometers across at the equator (JPL: equatorial radius 71492 km)
largest planet; Great Red Spot is a giant storm bigger than Earth; one day takes 9.9 hours

Saturn.lead: The ringed planet, about 120,500 kilometers across at the equator.
Saturn.story: Its rings are billions of chunks of ice and rock, from dust-sized grains to pieces as big as a house.

claims.text: about 120,500 kilometers across at the equator (JPL: equatorial radius 60268 km)
rings made of billions of small chunks of ice and rock, dust-sized grains to chunks as big as a house

Uranus.lead: A planet that spins tipped on its side, about 51,100 kilometers across at the equator.
Uranus.story: Voyager 2's visit in January 1986 is still the only one any spacecraft has made to Uranus.

claims.text: about 51,100 kilometers across at the equator (JPL: equatorial radius 25559 km)
rotates at a nearly 90-degree angle from the plane of its orbit
Jan. 24, 1986: Voyager 2 made the first and so far only visit to Uranus

Neptune.lead: The windiest planet in the solar system, about 49,500 kilometers across at the equator.
Neptune.story: Voyager 2 was the first spacecraft to fly by Neptune, in 1989, when a huge storm called the Great Dark Spot swirled in its southern hemisphere; that storm has since disappeared.

claims.text: about 49,500 kilometers across at the equator (JPL: equatorial radius 24764 km)
windiest world; Voyager 2 first spacecraft to fly by in 1989; Great Dark Spot in 1989, since disappeared

Io.lead: Jupiter's moon Io, the most volcanically active world in the solar system, about 3,640 kilometers across.
Io.story: Between them, the two Voyagers watched nine volcanoes erupting on Io.

claims.text: about 3,640 kilometers across (JPL: mean radius 1821.49 km)
most volcanically active world in the solar system
Together, the Voyagers observed the eruption of nine volcanoes on Io

Europa.lead: Jupiter's icy moon Europa, about 3,120 kilometers across.
Europa.story: Its water-ice surface is crisscrossed by dark, reddish-brown cracks, and there is strong evidence for an ocean of salty water beneath the crust.

claims.text: about 3,120 kilometers across (JPL: mean radius 1560.8 km)
water-ice surface crisscrossed by dark, reddish-brown cracks; strong evidence for an ocean of liquid salty water beneath its icy crust

Ganymede.lead: Jupiter's moon Ganymede, the largest moon in the solar system, about 5,260 kilometers across.
Ganymede.story: It is bigger than the planet Mercury and the dwarf planet Pluto.

claims.text: about 5,260 kilometers across (JPL: mean radius 2631.2 km)
largest moon in our solar system, bigger than the planet Mercury and dwarf planet Pluto

Callisto.lead: Jupiter's moon Callisto, about 4,820 kilometers across.
Callisto.story: Its rocky, icy surface is the oldest and most heavily cratered in the solar system.

claims.text: about 4,820 kilometers across (JPL: mean radius 2410.3 km)
rocky, icy surface is the oldest and most heavily cratered in our solar system

Amalthea.lead: Jupiter's small, irregularly shaped moon Amalthea, about 170 kilometers across.
Amalthea.story: NASA calls it the reddest object in the solar system.

claims.text: about 170 kilometers across (JPL: mean radius 83.5 km)
Amalthea is the reddest object in the solar system; irregularly shaped

Metis.lead: Metis, one of Jupiter's small inner moons, about 43 kilometers across.
Metis.story: It was discovered in 1979 by the Voyager science team.

claims.text: about 43 kilometers across (JPL: mean radius 21.5 km)
Metis (S/1979 J3) discovered 1979 by the Voyager Science Team

Titan.lead: Saturn's moon Titan, about 5,150 kilometers across.
Titan.story: The second largest moon in the solar system, it is wrapped in a thick, orange haze that makes its surface hard to see from space.

claims.text: about 5,150 kilometers across (JPL: mean radius 2574.76 km)
second largest moon in our solar system; thick, orange-colored haze makes the surface difficult to view from space

Rhea.lead: Saturn's moon Rhea, about 1,530 kilometers across.
Rhea.story: Saturn's second largest moon is made largely of water ice and is more heavily cratered than Dione and Tethys.

claims.text: about 1,530 kilometers across (JPL: mean radius 763.5 km)
second largest moon of Saturn; surface largely water ice; more heavily cratered than Dione and Tethys

Enceladus.lead: Saturn's small moon Enceladus, about 500 kilometers across.
Enceladus.story: Under its thick, icy shell lies a global ocean.

claims.text: about 500 kilometers across (JPL: mean radius 252.1 km)
Enceladus has a global ocean under a thick, icy shell

Tethys.lead: Saturn's moon Tethys, about 1,060 kilometers across.
Tethys.story: A huge valley called Ithaca Chasma runs across it from pole to pole.

claims.text: about 1,060 kilometers across (JPL: mean radius 531.1 km)
a valley called Ithaca Chasma runs pole to pole

Dione.lead: Saturn's moon Dione, about 1,120 kilometers across.
Dione.story: Its bright wispy streaks turned out, when Cassini flew past in 2005, to be walls of ice along canyons.

claims.text: about 1,120 kilometers across (JPL: mean radius 561.4 km)
Cassini flybys starting in 2005 showed the wisps as bright canyon ice walls

Iapetus.lead: Saturn's two-toned moon Iapetus, about 1,470 kilometers across.
Iapetus.story: Its leading side is as dark as coal, while its trailing side is much brighter.

claims.text: about 1,470 kilometers across (JPL: mean radius 734.3 km)
leading hemisphere as dark as coal; trailing hemisphere much brighter

Triton.lead: Neptune's moon Triton, about 2,710 kilometers across.
Triton.story: The only large moon that orbits against its planet's spin, it is one of the coolest objects in the solar system, and Voyager 2 found active geysers there.

claims.text: about 2,710 kilometers across (JPL: mean radius 1352.6 km)
only large moon that orbits opposite its planet's rotation; one of the coolest objects; Voyager 2 found active geysers

Saturn Rings.lead: Saturn's rings, made of billions of chunks of ice and rock.
Saturn Rings.story: The ring particles range from tiny, dust-sized icy grains to chunks as big as a house.

claims.text: rings made of billions of small chunks of ice and rock, dust-sized grains to chunks as big as a house

Jupiter Rings.lead: Jupiter's rings, which are hard to see and were a surprise when Voyager 1 found them.

claims.text: Discovered in 1979 by NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft, Jupiter's rings were a surprise; difficult to see
